passage: Lights-out had already gone in the boys' hostel, but Ojas was still sitting on his bed, turning his torch on and off. Kiran looked up from his bunk. "What's with you?" For a long moment Ojas said nothing. Then, very fast: "My parents are separating. Papa moved out last month. I haven't told anyone." His ears went hot. He waited for a joke. Kiran sat up and swung his legs down. "That's heavy, yaar. You've been carrying that alone?" Ojas nodded, eyes on the floor. "I thought you'd think I was weird." "Why would I?" Kiran said. "My uncle and aunty split. It was rough on my cousin." They talked in whispers until the warden's footsteps passed. Ojas slept better that night than he had in weeks.

qa.q: Who moved out last month, according to Ojas?
qa.a: His Papa moved out.

qa.q: What was Ojas afraid of before he spoke?
qa.a: He feared Kiran would mock him or think he was weird, which is why his ears went hot and he waited for a joke.

qa.q: Which reply from Kiran made opening up feel safe, and why?
qa.a: Asking whether Ojas had carried it alone showed he took it seriously, and sharing his cousin's story made Ojas feel less strange.

qa.q: What would change if Kiran had laughed?
qa.a: Ojas would likely have shut down and kept the secret even longer, feeling more alone and less willing to trust anyone.

grounding: Shows a teen taking the risky step of opening up to a peer about something painful, and the relief when it is received well.

passage:
Hi Yash,

Okay, this is weird to write, so I'm just going to type it before I chicken out.

When you asked on the phone last week how the new school was, I said "amazing, everyone's great." That wasn't true. I eat lunch in the library most days. Nobody's mean, I just haven't found my people, and I miss our gang so much it's embarrassing.

I didn't tell you because I thought you'd feel sorry for me, or think I'd become a loser here. But you're my oldest friend, and pretending with you felt worse than being lonely.

So, yeah. That's the truth. You don't have to fix anything. I just didn't want to lie to you anymore.

Your friend (who is fine, just not amazing),
Naveen

qa.q: Where does Naveen eat lunch most days at the new school?
qa.a: In the library, most days.

qa.q: Why did Naveen first tell Yash the school was amazing?
qa.a: Naveen was afraid Yash would feel sorry for Naveen or see Naveen as a loser, so the loneliness stayed hidden.

qa.q: What could Yash do after reading this email?
qa.a: Yash could thank Naveen for being honest, give Naveen a call, and keep in regular touch without rushing to fix things.

qa.q: If you were Yash, how might this email feel?
qa.a: It might sting that Naveen hid the truth, but it would also feel like a gift of trust from an old friend. 🤍

grounding: A teen writes to a close friend, taking the risk of dropping a brave front and admitting loneliness.

passage: "So, Simran, you asked about the hardest thing I did this year. It wasn't boards. It was one evening at Sneha's terrace. All my friends were talking about the trip to the hills, and I kept saying I'd 'check dates.' Truth was, my dad had lost his job in March and there was no money for trips. I'd been pretending for months: new excuses, fake busy. That evening I just... said it. My hands were shaking. I said, 'Guys, I can't afford it, and I've been lying because I was ashamed.' Nobody spoke for a second. Then Sneha said, 'Rukmini, why didn't you tell us?' and someone suggested a picnic at the lake instead. I cried a bit on the way home, but lighter, you know?"

qa.q: What had happened to Rukmini's dad in March?
qa.a: He had lost his job.

qa.q: How can you tell that telling the friends felt risky for Rukmini?
qa.a: Rukmini's hands were shaking, and Rukmini admits to months of shame and excuses.

qa.q: What could Rukmini's friends keep doing to support Rukmini?
qa.a: They could keep choosing low-cost plans like the lake picnic and check in quietly, without making money the centre of every talk.

qa.q: How might Sneha have felt when Rukmini spoke up?
qa.a: Sneha seems surprised and a little hurt that a friend carried this alone, but eager to help, asking why Rukmini hadn't told them.

grounding: A teen recounts opening up to friends about a hidden family hardship and how it deepened the friendship.

passage: I'm Damini, and I sit behind Yogesh in the Friday circle our class teacher runs. Usually he makes jokes when it's his turn. This Friday he didn't. He stared at the floor for a long time, and his leg kept bouncing. Then he said his father lost his job two months ago and that he's been pretending everything is normal because he didn't want anyone feeling sorry for him. His voice went thin at the end. Nobody laughed. I didn't know what to do, so I just said, 'Thanks for telling us.' A couple of others nodded. At lunch he sat with us instead of on the back bench. He seemed lighter, or maybe just tired. I'm honestly not sure which.

qa.q: How long ago did Yogesh's father lose his job?
qa.a: Two months ago.

qa.q: What might Yogesh's bouncing leg suggest before he spoke?
qa.a: It suggests he was nervous about the risk of telling the class something so personal.

qa.q: How could the class teacher support Yogesh after this?
qa.a: The teacher could check in with him privately, thank him for trusting the group, and keep the circle a place where no one mocks what is shared.

qa.q: How does Damini see the change in Yogesh at lunch?
qa.a: Damini notices he seems lighter or tired, but admits not being sure what he feels.

grounding: Shows a teenager taking the risk of dropping his joking cover to share something painful with classmates.

passage:
Monday: Chaitanya typed 'can we talk?' to Shalini and deleted it three times. For months he had been pretending the move to the new school was easy. It wasn't. He ate lunch in the library most days.
Wednesday: On the steps after tuition, he finally said it. 'I'm not okay here. I don't really have anyone except you.' His ears burned. Shalini didn't laugh. She was quiet, then said, 'I thought you didn't need anyone. You always seem so sorted.'
Saturday: She texted him a photo of a chess club notice: 'I'll come to the first one with you 🙂'. He saved the photo. For the first time in weeks, he didn't dread Monday.

qa.q: Where did Chaitanya eat lunch most days?
qa.a: In the library.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya's ears burn when he spoke?
qa.a: He felt exposed and embarrassed, since admitting he wasn't okay was a big emotional risk.

qa.q: What helped Chaitanya's openness pay off, and what could he do next?
qa.a: Shalini listened without laughing; next he could go to chess club with her and keep telling her honestly how things are.

qa.q: How did Shalini's picture of Chaitanya change?
qa.a: She had thought he was sorted and didn't need anyone, and learned he was actually lonely.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager moving from hiding loneliness to risking honesty with a friend, and what followed.

passage: "Seema, you think you have to be strong all the time? When I, your Omkar Mama, was sixteen, I had a stammer, worst on words starting with 'p'. I never talked in groups. My friends thought I was just quiet. One evening on the riverbank, my friend Sadanand asked why I never told stories. My heart was hammering. I could have made a joke. Instead I said, slowly, 'Because I'm scared of getting stuck in front of you.' He didn't laugh. He said, 'Then get stuck. We'll wait.' That was the first time I told a story in front of anyone."

qa.q: Which words did young Omkar's stammer affect most?
qa.a: Words starting with 'p'.

qa.q: What was young Omkar feeling when his heart was hammering?
qa.a: He felt scared and exposed, afraid of being judged if he told the truth.

qa.q: What turning point in the story came from opening up?
qa.a: Admitting his fear instead of joking, which led Sadanand to offer patience.

qa.q: How might Sadanand have felt when Omkar opened up?
qa.a: Touched and trusted, and glad to understand why his friend stayed quiet.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a teenager he took the risk of opening up about his stammer to a friend.

passage: The bus to school was packed, horns blaring outside, and Lakshmi, sixteen, had to shout to be heard. She'd been rehearsing this for weeks. "Anirban, can I tell you something?" He leaned closer. "Since we moved here, I've felt lonely all the time. Even when I'm laughing with the group. I pretend I'm fine." She stared at the window, scared of his face. The bus jolted. Anirban was quiet for a moment. "I had no idea," he said. "Thank you for telling me. Want to get chai after school? Just us, so we can actually talk." Lakshmi nodded, her eyes stinging.

qa.q: Where did Lakshmi tell Anirban?
qa.a: On the packed bus to school.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi stare at the window after speaking?
qa.a: She felt vulnerable and afraid of how Anirban would react to her honesty.

qa.q: What did Anirban do that honoured her risk?
qa.a: He thanked her and offered a quiet time to talk properly after school.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel learning his friend was lonely?
qa.a: Surprised and concerned, and glad she trusted him with it.

grounding: Shows a teenager taking the risk of admitting loneliness to a friend in a noisy, crowded place.

passage: Kavitha, seventeen, had told everyone the entrance exam went "fine". It hadn't. At the colony park bench, her friend Bhavna asked for the third time, "Really fine?" Kavitha's hands were cold. She could keep pretending, or she could say it. "I think I failed. And I'm scared that if I'm not an engineer, my parents will be disappointed in me for ever." She hadn't said those words even to herself. Bhavna didn't rush to fix it. "That sounds so heavy," she said. "Thank you for telling me." Kavitha cried, and felt lighter than she had in months.

qa.q: What had Kavitha told everyone about the exam?
qa.a: That it went "fine".

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling as her hands went cold?
qa.a: She felt anxious and exposed, weighing whether to risk telling the truth.

qa.q: What would you advise Kavitha next?
qa.a: Share the same fears with her parents or a school counsellor, now that she's said them out loud once.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel when Kavitha finally opens up?
qa.a: Trusted and caring, and relieved her friend stopped pretending.

grounding: Shows a teenager taking the risk of opening up fully to a friend about her fears.

passage:
"Arohi, can I tell you something?"
"Sure."
"You know how I always say I'm fine? That I don't care who I sit with?"
"Yeah, you're, like, the chillest person."
Ritu looked at her shoes. "I'm not. I eat lunch in the library because I don't know how to join people. I pretend to read."
Arohi was quiet.
"I've never told anyone. I thought if I said it, it'd be real."
"Ritu... I thought you liked being alone."
"I thought if I looked like I liked it, nobody would feel sorry for me."
Arohi slid closer. "Sit with me tomorrow. I'll save a place."
Ritu's eyes stung. "Promise you won't make it weird?"
"Promise," Arohi said, smiling. "Only a little weird."

qa.q: Where does Ritu eat lunch?
qa.a: In the library.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling as she looked at her shoes?
qa.a: She felt nervous and exposed, taking the risk of revealing her loneliness.

qa.q: How did Arohi respond, and why did it help?
qa.a: Arohi listened quietly and then offered to save Ritu a seat, turning the confession into a real step.

qa.q: How does Arohi's view of Ritu change?
qa.a: Arohi had thought Ritu liked being alone and now understands she was lonely and hiding it.

grounding: A teenager takes the risk of admitting her loneliness to a classmate.

passage: I'm Farida. Last year, before the science olympiad, everyone thought I was calm. I kept saying, "It's just a test." But I'd been waking up at three in the morning, heart racing, sure I'd let everyone down. One evening, sitting on the steps with Ira, I finally said it. "I'm scared I'm not as smart as people think." My voice went strange. I was waiting for her to laugh or to say, "Don't be silly." She didn't. She said, "I feel like that every time I paint." Then we just sat there. It didn't fix anything. But the next time I woke up at three, I texted her, and she replied a thumbs-up at seven, and somehow that was enough.

qa.q: What time was Farida waking up?
qa.a: At three in the morning.

qa.q: How did Farida feel when finally telling Ira the truth?
qa.a: Farida felt scared and exposed, voice going strange, expecting to be laughed at.

qa.q: What did Ira's reply do that helped?
qa.a: It met Farida's honesty with her own, so Farida felt less alone instead of judged.

qa.q: How might Ira have felt when Farida opened up?
qa.a: Ira may have felt trusted and moved, and safe enough to share her own worry.

grounding: A teenager recalls the risk of admitting to a friend the fear of not being smart enough.

passage:
Counsellor's note, peer support circle, Class 11. Vijay Rao.
Today's circle was on "what we hide." Most students shared small things. Then Gargi, who usually passes, raised her hand. She said her parents think she wants to be a doctor, and she has never told them she wants to study design, because she's scared they'll be disappointed in her. Her voice shook and she didn't look up. The room went quiet. One boy said, "Me too, but engineering." She laughed and cried at the same time. I thanked her for trusting the group. After the circle, I asked if she'd like help planning a conversation with her parents. She said yes. We meet on Thursday.

qa.q: What does Gargi want to study?
qa.a: Design.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when her voice shook?
qa.a: She felt scared and exposed, taking a big risk by sharing something she'd never told anyone.

qa.q: What did Vijay Rao do after the circle?
qa.a: He thanked her and offered help planning a conversation with her parents, with a meeting on Thursday.

qa.q: How might the boy who said "Me too" have felt?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved and braver, seeing that Gargi's openness made space for his own.

grounding: A counsellor records a teenager opening up in a support circle about hiding her real career wish.

passage:
Dear diary,
Today I told Keerthana the thing. The real thing. That since Papa left, I pretend at school that everything's normal, and it's exhausting.
I planned it for a week. I nearly backed out three times. My hands were cold. We were sitting on the steps behind the canteen and I said, "Can I tell you something that's not a joke?"
She put her phone away. That was the moment I knew I could.
I talked for maybe ten minutes. She didn't say anything wise. She just said, "That's so heavy. Thank you for telling me." Then she held out half her samosa.
I feel naked and lighter at the same time. Tomorrow I might regret it. Tonight I don't.
Rafiq

qa.q: Where were Rafiq and Keerthana sitting?
qa.a: On the steps behind the canteen.

qa.q: How does Rafiq feel after opening up?
qa.a: Rafiq feels exposed and lighter at the same time, and relieved for now.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana's response work so well?
qa.a: She put her phone away, listened, and thanked Rafiq without rushing to fix anything, which made it safe to keep talking.

qa.q: What might Keerthana have felt as she listened?
qa.a: She probably felt moved and trusted, and a little unsure what to say, so she simply stayed kind.

grounding: A teen's diary about taking the risk of telling a friend something deeply personal.

passage:
After the Holi fair in their small town, Jaya and Rehana sat on the steps of the closed post office, colour still on their arms.
Rehana was talking about the stalls. Jaya kept twisting her dupatta.
"Rehana, you know how I'm always the one who jokes?"
"Yes, you're the joker."
"I don't feel like a joker. Since Dadi died, I feel scared all the time that everyone else will go too. I've never said that out loud."
The silence felt very long. A tractor went past.
Then Rehana leaned her shoulder into Jaya's. "I think about my father's heart all the time," she said quietly. "I never say it either."
They sat until the lamps came on. Jaya's knees had stopped shaking.

qa.q: Where did Jaya and Rehana sit after the fair?
qa.a: On the steps of the closed post office.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling as she twisted her dupatta?
qa.a: She felt nervous and afraid of how Rehana would react to her real fear.

qa.q: How did Rehana make it safe for Jaya to keep going?
qa.a: She leaned in and shared her own worry about her father, showing Jaya she was not alone.

qa.q: What would change if Rehana had laughed it off?
qa.a: Jaya might have felt ashamed and gone back to joking, keeping her fear hidden longer.

grounding: Shows a teen taking the risk of revealing a deep fear to a friend in a small-town setting.

passage: After football practice in Amsterdam, Lars and Mateo sat on the canal wall eating fries, as they did every Tuesday. Mateo was talking about Saturday's party with the older boys from Year 12. Lars kept picking at the paper cone. "Can I say something a bit embarrassing?" Mateo shrugged. Lars's heart was pounding. "Since you started hanging out with them, I've felt left behind. Like I'm the friend you have on Tuesdays. I didn't want to sound needy, so I just said nothing." He stared at the water, waiting for a joke. Mateo put his fries down. "I didn't know. That must have felt rubbish." He paused. "Come on Saturday. And Tuesdays stay ours." Lars let out a long breath.

qa.q: What were Lars and Mateo eating on the canal wall?
qa.a: They were eating fries.

qa.q: What was Lars feeling as he stared at the water, waiting?
qa.a: He felt anxious and exposed, afraid Mateo would laugh at him for sounding needy.

qa.q: What did Lars do that made the risk worth taking?
qa.a: He named his feeling plainly and without blaming Mateo, which made it easy for Mateo to respond kindly.

qa.q: How does Mateo experience Lars's confession?
qa.a: Mateo is surprised, not having known, and responds with care, inviting Lars on Saturday and keeping Tuesdays.

grounding: Shows a teenager taking the risk of telling a close friend he has felt left behind.
